title: Driver lines for studying associative learning in Drosophila
abstract: The mushroom body (MB) is the center for associative learning in insects. In Drosophila, intersectional split-GAL4 drivers and electron microscopy (EM) connectomes have laid the foundation for precise interrogation of the MB neural circuits. However, investigation of many cell types upstream and downstream of the MB has been hindered due to lack of specific driver lines. Here we describe a new collection of over 800 split-GAL4 and split-LexA drivers that cover approximately 300 cell types, including sugar sensory neurons, putative nociceptive ascending neurons, olfactory and thermo-/hygro-sensory projection neurons, interneurons connected with the MB-extrinsic neurons, and various other cell types. We characterized activation phenotypes for a subset of these lines and identified a sugar sensory neuron line most suitable for reward substitution. Leveraging the thousands of confocal microscopy images associated with the collection, we analyzed neuronal morphological stereotypy and discovered that one set of mushroom body output neurons, MBON08/MBON09, exhibits striking individuality and asymmetry across animals. In conjunction with the EM connectome maps, the driver lines reported here offer a powerful resource for functional dissection of neural circuits for associative learning in adult Drosophila.

elife_assessment.summary: This important collection of over 800 new cell type-specific driver lines will be an invaluable resource for researchers studying associative learning in Drosophila. Thoroughly characterized and well documented, this collection will permit researchers to selectively target neurons that deliver information to, or receive it from, the memory center of the fly brain called the Mushroom Body. Given the wealth of new drivers and the genetic access they provide to over 300 cell types, this compelling work will be of interest not only to researchers studying the mechanisms of associative learning but more generally to those dissecting sensorimotor circuits in the fly nervous system.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2024 eLife article is already showing clear scholarly traction: it sits in the top 10% of cited works for its field and year, has 11 OpenAlex citations, and has been reused in 12 downstream works. The pattern of reuse, together with eLife’s assessment of the resource as “Important” and “Compelling,” points to a methodological paper that is being taken up quickly by researchers working on Drosophila neural circuitry and associative learning.

Full narrative

Driver lines for studying associative learning in Drosophila addresses a practical bottleneck in mushroom body research: while connectomic maps and split-GAL4 tools have made it possible to probe the fly memory circuit with precision, many upstream and downstream cell types have remained difficult to target. The article responds by introducing a large collection of more than 800 split-GAL4 and split-LexA drivers spanning roughly 300 cell types, giving the field a substantially expanded toolkit for circuit interrogation.

The article’s influence is shaping up as primarily methodological rather than narrowly topical. Its reuse profile is especially telling: downstream citing works are overwhelmingly preprints, clustered in Drosophila neuroscience and related sensory-behavior studies, which suggests that the driver collection is being incorporated early into active experimental pipelines. The presence of an RRID-rich record also reinforces its role as a reusable community resource, not just a single-study report.

That early uptake is also consistent with the citation landscape. Although the absolute citation count is still modest, the field-normalized standing is strong, indicating that the paper is accruing attention faster than would be expected for a work of this age and subject area. The citing record is concentrated in neuroscience and insect physiology, with multiple recent preprints using the article as enabling infrastructure for studies of learning, nociception, valence, and neuromodulatory circuits in Drosophila.

The surrounding stewardship signals strengthen the case for durability. The work is gold open access, funded by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and its associated materials are deposited in open repositories. Taken together, the record shows a well-documented and openly available resource paper that is already functioning as an anchor for new experimental work on associative learning and related fly-brain circuits.

At the same time, the public-facing record is still relatively quiet: there are no documented event-data mentions in the sources provided, so the clearest evidence of impact remains scholarly reuse and citation. In other words, this is a paper whose influence is visible first in the research it enables, rather than in broader public conversation.
